================================================================================
1. EXECUTIVE SUMMARY & OVERVIEW
================================================================================

WHAT IS ANTE?

Ante is a professional CLI tool for working with language models and AI systems.
It provides a comprehensive ecosystem for:

- Interacting with multiple LLM providers
- Managing complex multi-step tasks with sub-agents
- Persistent knowledge storage via memory systems
- Rich tool ecosystem for extending capabilities
- Flexible configuration and preferences
- Professional interfaces (TUI and headless modes)
- Seamless integration with coding workflows

CORE CAPABILITIES:

✓ Multi-provider LLM support (OpenAI, Anthropic, and third-party)
✓ Advanced sub-agent system for task delegation
✓ Persistent memory across sessions
✓ 20+ built-in tools for file operations, coding, web access, etc.
✓ Interactive TUI and headless modes
✓ Flexible configuration and customization
✓ Integration with git, bash, and development workflows
✓ Context management and token optimization

KEY ADVANTAGES:

- No external dependencies for core functionality
- Unified interface for multiple LLM providers
- Intelligent context and memory management
- Support for specialized tasks via sub-agents
- Professional-grade error handling
- Comprehensive documentation and examples
- Active development and community support

Ante models agent interactions as a hierarchy of concepts, connected by a typed message-passing protocol.
Concept hierarchy
└── Session
Description
A git repo or root directory. Can have multiple sessions.
One episode of interaction between user and Ante. Manages dialog state, token usage, and context compaction.
One piece of work the user wants to accomplish. Can span multiple turns.
One back-and-forth with the agent. Starts with user input, ends with agent message or approval request.
One interaction from agent with LLM. Handles tool calls and other mechanics.
Generally, if there is no approval interruption, one task consists of one turn.
Protocol: Ops and Events
Ante uses a message-passing protocol between the client (TUI or headless runner) and the daemon. Operations (
) flow from client to daemon, and events (
) flow from daemon to client.

Context management
Ante automatically manages context windows:
Token budget
— Each turn tracks token usage against the model’s context limit
Auto-compaction
— When the dialog approaches the context limit, Ante uses the LLM to summarize the conversation history, preserving important context while freeing tokens
Tool result trimming
— Large tool outputs are automatically trimmed to fit within budget
Permissions
Ante has a permission system that gates tool execution:
Tools marked
requires_approval
prompt the user before execution
All tools execute without approval
In the TUI, you approve or deny each tool call interactively. In headless mode,
is implied (all tools auto-approved).

3. SYSTEM ARCHITECTURE
================================================================================

Ante is built on a modular, extensible architecture:

Architecture - Ante

Agent Organization (Experimental)

Offline Mode (Experimental)

Model & Provider Catalog

Architecture
Ante Preview
Ante Preview
Ante follows a clean separation of concerns with a client-daemon architecture. The UI and core logic are decoupled through message passing, making it possible to swap frontends (TUI, headless) without changing the underlying engine.
Client-Daemon split
┌────────────────┐ ┌─────────────────────────────┐
│ Client │ Op │ Daemon │
│ │ ───────▶ │ │
│ TUI (ratatui) │ │ Session ─▶ Turn ─▶ Step │
│ or Headless │ ◀─────── │ │
│ │ Evt │ Tools Providers Store │
└────────────────┘ └─────────────────────────────┘
— The user-facing layer. Either the ratatui-based TUI or the headless CLI runner. Sends
operations and renders
— The core engine. Receives operations, manages sessions, dispatches to LLM providers, schedules tool execution, and emits events.
— Bounded async channels (Tokio) connect client and daemon within the same process. Message IDs enable tracing across the boundary.
LLM providers
Ante is provider-agnostic. Each provider implements a common interface for sending prompts and receiving streaming responses.
Wire Format
Messages API
Claude family
Chat Completions / Responses
GPT-4o, o1, etc.
Gemini family
OpenAI-compatible
Grok models
Open Router
OpenAI-compatible
Multiple providers
GGUF models
Providers are resolved from a catalog at session init time. The user can override via CLI flags (
) or persistent settings.
Authentication
— Set via environment variables (
ANTHROPIC_API_KEY
OPENAI_API_KEY
— Interactive OAuth flow supported for Anthropic and OpenAI, handled through the TUI

Op::NewSession
with model, provider, and policy

to start a task

which communicates with the LLM

6. SUB-AGENTS & SPECIALIZED SKILLS
================================================================================

Ante includes sophisticated sub-agent and skill systems for specialized tasks.

SUB-AGENTS OVERVIEW:

Ante uses sub-agents to delegate and manage specialized tasks:

Sub-Agents - Ante
Eval & Benchmark
Architecture
Agent Organization (Experimental)
Offline Mode
Offline Mode (Experimental)
Interactive TUI
Headless Mode
Model & Provider Catalog
Preferences
Adding a 3rd Party Provider
Ante Preview
Ante Preview
Sub-agents are specialized agents that the main agent can spawn to handle complex, multi-step tasks. Each sub-agent runs with its own prompt, tool set, and optional model override.
Built-in sub-agents
Ante ships with two built-in sub-agents:
A general-purpose agent for researching complex questions, searching for code, and executing multi-step tasks. The main agent delegates to this when it needs to perform a search it isn’t confident about completing in a few tries.
A fast agent specialized for codebase exploration. It can quickly find files by patterns, search code for keywords, and answer structural questions about the codebase.
Creating custom sub-agents
Create a markdown file in
~/.ante/agents/
with YAML frontmatter:
"security-reviewer"
description
"Reviews code for security vulnerabilities and OWASP top 10 issues"
You are a security-focused code reviewer. Analyze the provided code for:
Injection vulnerabilities (SQL, command, XSS)
Authentication and authorization flaws
Sensitive data exposure
Security misconfiguration
Known vulnerable dependencies
Provide findings with severity ratings and remediation steps.
Frontmatter fields
Description
Unique identifier for the agent
description
What this agent does (shown to the main agent for delegation decisions)
Override the LLM model for this agent
Restrict which tools this agent can use
Display color in the TUI
How sub-agents work
When the main agent encounters a task that matches a sub-agent’s description, it uses the
tool to spawn the sub-agent:
The main agent evaluates available sub-agents and their descriptions
It delegates the task via the
tool with a detailed prompt
The sub-agent runs independently with its own context
The result is returned to the main agent, which incorporates it into the conversation
┌────────────┐ Task ┌──────────────┐
│ Main Agent │ ────────────▶ │ Sub-Agent │
│ │ ◀──────────── │ (Explorer) │
│ │ Result └──────────────┘
│ │ Task ┌──────────────┐
│ │ ────────────▶ │ Sub-Agent │
│ │ ◀──────────── │ (General) │
└────────────┘ Result └──────────────┘
Sub-agents are discovered from:
Built-in agents (General, Explorer)
~/.ante/agents/
User-defined agents are loaded alongside the built-in ones. All available agents are registered at session initialization time.

Skills are folders of instructions, scripts, and resources that extend Ante’s capabilities. They follow the open
Agent Skills
format, making them portable across compatible agent products.
Creating a skill
A skill is a directory containing a
└── SKILL.md
uses YAML frontmatter followed by Markdown instructions:
description
Create a git commit with a descriptive message following conventional commit format.
Look at the current git diff and create a commit with a clear,
descriptive message that follows conventional commit format.
to stage relevant files first.
Example: review skill with tools and references
├── SKILL.md
└── references/
└── checklist.md
description
Review code changes for bugs, security issues, and style. Use when the user asks for a code review.
allowed-tools
Review the code at $ARGUMENTS for:
Bugs and logic errors
Security vulnerabilities
Style and idiom issues
Missing error handling
references/checklist.md
) for the full review checklist.
Provide a summary with specific line references.
Skill directories
~/.ante/skills/
User-level (available in all projects)
agents/skills/
Project-level (available in this project)
.ante/skills/
Project-level (available in this project)
.claude/skills/
Project-level (available in this project)
SKILL.md frontmatter
must start with a YAML frontmatter block delimited by
. The block can be empty, but the delimiters are required.
Description
Parent directory name
Identifier for the skill. If omitted, the skill directory name is used.
description
First paragraph of body
What this skill does and when to use it. If omitted, extracted from the first paragraph of the Markdown body.
argument-hint
Hint text shown to the user for expected arguments (e.g.
user-invocable
Whether the skill can be invoked by the user via slash command. Set to
for skills intended only for model invocation.
disable-model-invocation
, prevents the model from invoking this skill automatically.
allowed-tools
YAML list of pre-approved tools the skill can use (e.g.
Bash(git diff -- *)
Arbitrary key-value pairs for additional metadata.
Optional directories
Skills can include additional resources alongside
├── SKILL.md # Required — instructions
├── scripts/ # Executable code the agent can run
├── references/ # Additional docs loaded on demand
└── assets/ # Templates, schemas, data files
— Self-contained scripts (Python, Bash, etc.) the agent can execute
references/
— Detailed documentation loaded only when needed, keeping the main instructions lean
— Static resources like templates, schemas, or lookup tables
How skills are discovered
Skills are discovered from multiple directories in precedence order.
Later directories override earlier ones
if they share a skill name:
System-level (built-in skills)
~/.ante/skills/
(user-level)
agents/skills/
(project-level)
.ante/skills/
(project-level)
.claude/skills/
(project-level)
A project-level skill overrides a user-level skill of the same name. If multiple project-level directories contain a skill with the same name, the one discovered last wins.
Using skills
Invoke a skill during a session with the slash syntax:
Or with arguments:
/review src/core/session.rs
placeholder in the skill instructions will be replaced with whatever you pass after the skill name.
The Agent Skills format is an open standard supported by multiple agent products. See the
full specification
for details on naming conventions, progressive disclosure, and validation.

8. MEMORY & CONTEXT MANAGEMENT
================================================================================

Ante's memory system enables intelligent, persistent context management:

Memory - Ante
Eval & Benchmark
Architecture
Agent Organization (Experimental)
Offline Mode
Offline Mode (Experimental)
Interactive TUI
Headless Mode
Model & Provider Catalog
Preferences
Adding a 3rd Party Provider
Ante Preview
Ante Preview
Ante has a persistent memory system that lets the agent build up knowledge across conversations. Insights, patterns, and lessons learned are stored in memory files and automatically loaded into the system prompt for future sessions.
How it works
Each project has a memory directory (typically
.claude/projects/<project-path>/memory/
). The key file is
— its contents are injected into the system prompt at the start of every conversation.
Automatic behavior
As the agent works on your project, it:
existing memory files to build on previous experience
new insights when it encounters common mistakes or useful patterns
or removes memories that turn out to be wrong or outdated
The main memory file. Its first 200 lines are included in the system prompt. Keep it concise — link to separate topic files for details.
# Project patterns
`anyhow::Result`
for all fallible functions
Tests go in
`#[cfg(test)]`
modules alongside code
debugging.md
debugging.md
) for common issues
# Known issues
The auth module needs refactoring (tracked in #123)
Topic files
For detailed notes, create separate files and reference them from
├── MEMORY.md # Main file (auto-loaded, max 200 lines)
├── debugging.md # Detailed debugging notes
├── patterns.md # Code patterns and conventions
└── architecture.md # Architecture decisions
The memory system follows these principles:
is truncated after 200 lines, so keep it focused
— Organize by topic, not chronologically
— Update or remove outdated information
— Record what worked, what didn’t, and why
Memory is per-project
Memory is scoped to each project directory. Different projects have independent memory directories. This means the agent’s accumulated knowledge about your React frontend won’t interfere with its knowledge about your Rust backend.
Manual editing
You can edit memory files directly — they are plain markdown. The agent can also update them using the
tools during a session.
On this page
How it works
Automatic behavior
Topic files
Memory is per-project
Manual editing

Memory - Ante


MEMORY BEST PRACTICES:

- Use /Users/kooshapari/.ante/projects/[project]/memory/MEMORY.md for persistent
  notes that carry across conversations
- Keep MEMORY.md concise (200-line limit)
- Create topic-specific files for detailed information
- Update memory as you learn patterns and insights
- Link between memory files for navigation
- Archive outdated or incorrect information

Headless Mode
Ante Preview
Ante Preview
Headless mode runs Ante without the TUI — it processes a prompt, executes the task, and exits. This is ideal for scripting, CI/CD pipelines, and automated workflows.
Basic usage
Provide a prompt as an argument:
"explain what this project does"
"add tests for the auth module"
Stdin input
Pipe content from stdin:
src/main.rs
"review this code for bugs"
Combine stdin with a prompt argument:
"function add(a, b) { return a + b }"
"add TypeScript types"
When both stdin and a prompt argument are provided, they are concatenated (stdin first, then the prompt).
CLI reference
ante [OPTIONS] [--prompt <PROMPT>]
Description
--prompt <PROMPT>
The prompt to run
--model <MODEL>
Override the model name
--provider <PROVIDER>
Override the API provider
--output-format <FORMAT>
Output format:
--system-prompt <PROMPT>
Replace the default system prompt entirely
--append-system-prompt <TEXT>
Append text to the system prompt
--allowed-tools <TOOLS>...
Only allow these tools (space-separated)
--disallowed-tools <TOOLS>...
Disallow these tools (space-separated)
Run a verification pass after the main task completes
Output formats
Minimal (default)
Shows only agent messages, info, and errors:
"what does this project do"
Shows all events in a human-readable format with ANSI colors:
--output-format
"fix the type error in main.rs"
Outputs every event as a JSON object (one per line), suitable for machine consumption:
--output-format
"list all TODO comments"
Verification check
flag runs a second pass after the main task, asking the agent to review its own work:
"refactor the auth module to use async/await"
The verification pass will:
Review what was accomplished against the original request
Complete anything missing or incomplete
Optimize where possible without affecting correctness
Context enrichment
In headless mode, Ante automatically appends the current directory’s folder structure to your prompt. This gives the agent awareness of the project layout without you needing to describe it.
Headless behavior notes
Streaming is disabled
— Responses are buffered for cleaner output
Yolo policy is implied
— All tool calls are auto-approved (no interactive prompts)
Authentication is checked eagerly
— If the provider isn’t authenticated, Ante exits immediately with an error
CI: lint and fix
"run cargo clippy and fix all warnings"
Code generation
claude-sonnet-4-5-20250514
"add comprehensive unit tests for src/core/session.rs"
Restricted tools
# Read-only analysis — no file writes or shell access
--allowed-tools
"analyze the codebase architecture and summarize it"
Pipe a diff for review
"review this diff for bugs and security issues"

Ante Preview
Ante Preview
Launch Ante without a prompt to enter the interactive TUI:
The TUI is built with
and provides a rich chat interface directly in your terminal. It renders inline (up to 24 lines) and uses debounced rendering at approximately 100fps for smooth output.
Key features
Chat interface
The main view shows a conversation between you and the agent. Type your prompt in the input area and press Enter to send. The agent’s responses stream in real-time with markdown rendering.
Tool approval
When the agent wants to execute a tool that requires approval (like
), you’ll see an approval prompt. You can:
the tool call
it and the agent will adjust its approach
When the agent proposes file edits, Ante switches to a fullscreen diff view on an alternate screen. You can review the exact changes before approving.
Model and provider selection
Use the built-in selectors to switch models or providers during a session without restarting.
Theme selection
Ante includes a theme system for consistent styling. Choose a theme through the theme dialog.
Keyboard shortcuts
Send message
Interrupt current task / Exit
Cancel current input
CLI flags for TUI mode
You can customize the TUI session with flags:
# Use a specific model
claude-sonnet-4-5-20250514
# Use a specific provider
# Override the system prompt
--system-prompt
"You are a Python expert"
# Append to the system prompt
--append-system-prompt
"Always use type hints"
# Restrict available tools
--allowed-tools
# Remove specific tools
--disallowed-tools
Streaming is enabled by default in TUI mode for real-time response rendering. To disable it, set the
ANTE_DISABLE_STREAMING
environment variable:
ANTE_DISABLE_STREAMING

Eval & Benchmark
Ante Preview
Ante Preview
Evaluation is the backbone of building a reliable AI agent. We were practicing the same principles Anthropic later laid out in
Demystifying Evals for AI Agents
before they published it.
Most of the magic comes from the model — but the agent harness is the critical conduit between human and AI.
We evaluate the
and how well it channels the model’s power — not the model itself.
Which is why we chose
Terminal Bench
and its real-world complex task environment.
Drawn from the practices in
Demystifying Evals for AI Agents
Start early, start simple.
A small but honest eval set drawn from actual failures beats a large contrived one.
Grade outcomes, not trajectories.
Did the agent solve the problem? Especially for a terminal agent, many correct paths exist.
Isolate and reproduce.
Every eval run starts clean. When a score drops, we know it reflects a real regression.
Why Terminal Bench/Harbor
Terminal Bench
as our primary external benchmark for following reasons:
Unambiguous task specs, deterministic grading where possible, and isolated execution environments.
Focused on core capability.
Can the agent accomplish real tasks in a real shell? Reading context, reasoning, acting, verifying — the exact loop we are building Ante around.
Terminal Bench 2.0 results
Topped the Terminal Bench 1.0 leaderboard in 2025
Topped the Terminal Bench 2.0 leaderboard in 2026 as verified agent and remain best in class for Gemini (February 2026)
Ante's fundamental abstractions, and the Op/Evt message protocol that connects them

================================================================================
11. BEST PRACTICES & PATTERNS
================================================================================

TOOL USAGE BEST PRACTICES:

1. Always verify tool availability before using
2. Check file paths are absolute, not relative
3. Quote paths containing spaces with double quotes
4. Use parallel tool calls when operations are independent
5. Chain dependent operations with && in bash
6. Handle errors gracefully and provide context

BASH EXECUTION BEST PRACTICES:

✓ Always quote file paths with spaces: "/path with spaces/file.txt"
✓ Use && for dependent commands: cmd1 && cmd2
✓ Use ; for sequential commands: cmd1; cmd2
✓ Set timeouts for long operations: timeout 600000ms for 10 minutes
✓ Use unbuffered output for background processes: python3 -u script.py &
✓ Avoid cd - use absolute paths instead

FILE OPERATIONS:

✓ Read file before editing with Edit tool
✓ Use Read with offset/limit for large files (2000+ lines)
✓ Use Write for creating new files
✓ Use Edit for modifying existing files
✓ Always verify files exist after writing

GIT OPERATIONS:

✓ Use git status before making changes
✓ Review git diff to understand all modifications
✓ Use HEREDOC for multi-line commit messages
✓ Cannot use interactive git flags (-i)
✓ Must manually resolve merge conflicts before committing
✓ Run git status after committing to verify success

MEMORY MANAGEMENT:

✓ Check memory files at start of session
✓ Update MEMORY.md with learned insights
✓ Create topic-specific memory files for detailed notes
✓ Keep memory organized semantically
✓ Link between related memory files
✓ Regularly review and remove outdated information

SUB-AGENT DELEGATION:

✓ Use explore for understanding codebase structure
✓ Use task for complex multi-step operations
✓ Provide clear context and requirements
✓ Wait for results before dependent tasks
✓ Review sub-agent output thoroughly

TASK MANAGEMENT:

✓ Use TodoWrite for multi-step tasks (3+ steps)
✓ Create specific, actionable task items
✓ Mark tasks in_progress before starting
✓ Complete tasks immediately after finishing
✓ Only one task should be in_progress at a time
✓ Remove tasks that are no longer relevant

PROVIDER & MODEL SELECTION:

✓ Choose providers based on task requirements
✓ Use faster/cheaper models for simple tasks
✓ Reserve advanced models for complex reasoning
✓ Consider cost vs capability tradeoffs
✓ Test with multiple models if accuracy critical
✓ Implement fallback providers for reliability

CONTEXT OPTIMIZATION:

✓ Keep responses concise and focused
✓ Avoid redundancy in explanations
✓ Use code references (file:line) for navigation
✓ Batch related operations to reduce token usage
✓ Leverage memory to avoid repeating information

================================================================================
12. CONSTRAINTS & LIMITATIONS
================================================================================

ENVIRONMENT CONSTRAINTS:

• Non-interactive shell - no user input prompts
• User-defined aliases not available (use full command names)
• Commands requiring editors (git commit, git rebase) need special flags
• Background processes may buffer output without unbuffered mode
• Some commands have platform-specific behavior

TOOL CONSTRAINTS:

• File paths must be absolute, not relative
• File paths with spaces must be quoted: "/path/with spaces/file"
• Bash default timeout: 2 minutes (can increase to 10 minutes max)
• Tool output limited to 30,000 characters
• Some tools have rate limits or usage quotas
• Find, grep, cat should use dedicated tools instead of bash

CONTEXT & MEMORY CONSTRAINTS:

• Context window is finite but managed via auto-summarization
• MEMORY.md limited to 200 lines (keep concise)
• Large files should use Read with offset/limit parameters
• Auto-memory directory per project at ~/.ante/projects/[path]/memory/

SECURITY CONSTRAINTS:

• Never use sudo without explicit authorization
• Avoid running untrusted code
• Validate all user input at system boundaries
• Be cautious with credentials and sensitive data
• Do not perform destructive operations without confirmation

GIT CONSTRAINTS:

• Cannot use interactive git commands (no -i flag)
• Must use non-interactive alternatives
• Cannot use editor-dependent git commands
• Must manually resolve merge conflicts
• Pre-commit hooks may modify staged files

MODEL & PROVIDER CONSTRAINTS:

• Some providers have rate limits
• Token usage varies significantly by model
• Context window sizes differ between providers
• Pricing varies by provider and model
• Some models may be unavailable in certain regions
• API keys and credentials required for some providers

================================================================================
13. API & INTEGRATION DETAILS
================================================================================

TOOL FUNCTION REFERENCE:

READING FILES:
- Reads file from filesystem (supports images, PDFs)
- Parameters: path (absolute), offset (optional), limit (optional)
- Returns: file contents with line numbers (cat -n format)

WRITING FILES:
- Creates or overwrites files
- Must read file first if already exists
- Parameters: file_path (absolute), content (string)
- Returns: success/failure status

EDITING FILES:
- Modifies existing file with exact string replacement
- Must read file first using Read tool
- Parameters: file_path, old_string, new_string, replace_all (optional)
- Returns: success/failure with context

BASH EXECUTION:
- Executes bash commands with optional timeout
- Quote file paths with spaces
- Parameters: command (string), description (optional), timeout (optional)
- Returns: stdout, stderr, exit code
- Default timeout: 2 minutes, max: 10 minutes

GREP SEARCH:
- Ripgrep-based full-text search
- Supports regex patterns and file filtering
- Parameters: pattern, path (optional), type (optional), output_mode
- Output modes: files_with_matches, content (with context), count

GLOB FILE SEARCH:
- Fast file pattern matching
- Glob patterns: "**/*.js", "src/**/*.ts"
- Parameters: pattern, path (optional)
- Returns: sorted file paths by modification time

TODO MANAGEMENT:
- Create and manage task lists for tracking progress
- Use for multi-step tasks (3+ steps)
- States: pending, in_progress, completed
- Parameters: todos (array of objects with content, activeForm, status)

WEB FETCH:
- Fetch and analyze web content
- Converts HTML to markdown
- Parameters: url (fully-formed), prompt (extraction request)
- Returns: processed content with AI analysis

BACKGROUND EXECUTION:
- Run long-running commands in background with &
- Use BashOutput to retrieve results
- Returns: shell_id for tracking
- Output redirected to ~/.ante/bash_output_TIMESTAMP.txt

KILL SHELL:
- Terminate background shell process
- Parameters: shell_id (from Bash tool output)
- Returns: success/failure status

CODE REFERENCES:

When referencing code, use format: file_path:line_number
Example: src/services/process.ts:712

This allows easy navigation to source code location.

EXAMPLE PATTERNS:

Reading and checking file existence:
```
Read("/path/to/file.ts") → Verify file exists → Edit with changes
```

Parallel tool calls:
```
[Call 1] Bash "git status" → [Call 2] Bash "git diff" → Analyze results
```

Dependent operations:
```
[Call 1] Bash "mkdir dir && cd dir" → [Call 2] Write file in that dir
```

Todo management for complex tasks:
```
1. Create todos for all steps
2. Mark first as in_progress
3. Complete each step
4. Mark as completed immediately
5. Move to next todo
```

================================================================================
14. COMMON PATTERNS & WORKFLOWS
================================================================================

WORKFLOW: Reading and Modifying Code

1. Use Read to examine file
2. Understand current implementation
3. Use Edit to make targeted changes
4. Verify changes with Read (optional)
5. Test or verify changes work

WORKFLOW: Multi-Step Task Management

1. Create todos for all steps with TodoWrite
2. Mark first todo in_progress
3. Perform the work
4. Mark complete immediately
5. Update todo to next step
6. Repeat for all steps

WORKFLOW: Parallel Independent Operations

1. Identify independent operations (no dependencies)
2. Make all tool calls in single message
3. Wait for results
4. Proceed with dependent operations if any

WORKFLOW: Git Commit with Multiple Changes

1. git status (check what changed)
2. git diff (review all changes)
3. git log (understand commit message style)
4. git add files (stage relevant files)
5. git commit -m "message" (create commit)
6. git status (verify success)

WORKFLOW: Exploring Unknown Codebase

1. Use Glob to find key files
2. Use Grep to search for patterns
3. Read key files to understand structure
4. Use Task agent for complex exploration
5. Update MEMORY.md with findings

WORKFLOW: Managing Context in Large Codebases

1. Read and understand the specific area needed
2. Use Grep for targeted searches
3. Keep file reads focused and limited
4. Use memory to store patterns and insights
5. Reference specific file:line in explanations
